title: The oldest poems
hook: among the oldest Buddhist verses, first put into English in full in 1881

segments.voice: Yesterday the Long Discourses closed. Your line: the long way home. Today, a new collection, and a much older sound.

In 1881, in Oxford, a volume came off the press: the tenth book in a series called the Sacred Books of the East. Inside were two Buddhist texts in English, side by side. One was the Dhammapada, translated by Max Muller. The other was a collection of poems, translated from the Pali by a Danish scholar named Viggo Fausboll. Some readers think a few of those poems belong to the oldest layers of the Buddhist canon. Today, that second book opens. Today's word: Sutta Nipata.
screen: `OXFORD, 1881.` → `A DANISH SCHOLAR'S TRANSLATION.` → `A SECOND BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata means something like the collection of discourses, or the gathering of suttas. It's a small book of short pieces, most of them in verse, sorted into five chapters. Some you may have met: the discourse on loving-kindness, the discourse on blessings, the rhinoceros poem. Why do some scholars call parts of it old? The language of some verses is archaic, closer to older Indian poetry. The fourth and fifth chapters, the Chapter of Eights and the Way to the Beyond, are explained line by line by another text inside the canon itself, the Niddesa. To these scholars, a commentary inside the canon suggests the poems were already old and already puzzling while the canon was still being shaped. And the life in them is spare: wanderers, forests, rivers, almost no buildings, very little organization. Some read that as a window onto the earliest days. Others are more cautious and say old verses and newer ones sit side by side. So this path reads it slowly. These are poems meant to be said aloud and remembered, with refrains that come back verse after verse, the way a song comes back to its chorus. Ahead: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros, a plowman, a spirit with a threat, and a long list of blessings.
screen: `THE COLLECTION OF DISCOURSES` · `FIVE CHAPTERS, MOSTLY VERSE` · `A COMMENTARY INSIDE THE CANON` · `POEMS MEANT TO BE SAID ALOUD` · then, large: `OLD WORDS.`

segments.voice: Read one verse aloud, from the other book in that 1881 volume, Max Muller's Dhammapada, a line that calls itself old. Say it slowly, in a normal speaking voice: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule. Say it once more, a little slower, and notice the sound in your mouth and the quiet after it, then sit with the breath.
screen: `FOR HATRED DOES NOT CEASE BY HATRED AT ANY TIME.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata. The collection of discourses: a small book of short pieces, mostly verse, some of them very old. Today's word.
Your line: old words. An old sentence, heard once again. Day five hundred seventy-six, done.

screen: `DAY 576 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SNAKE SHEDS ITS SKIN.`

howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, especially the discourses on loving-kindness, blessings and the jewel, are among the texts chanted in Theravada temples and homes, and the collection is studied in monasteries.

chat.says: Why do some scholars think parts of the Sutta Nipata are so old?
options: Old language, and a commentary on it sits inside the canon itself.
It was found carved in stone at the Buddha's birthplace.

chat.meaning: Some scholars point to archaic language and to the Niddesa, a commentary inside the canon on chapters four and five; others say old and newer verses mix.

notes: Hook says 1881 was the first full English translation: Mutu Coomaraswamy published a partial English Sutta Nipata in 1874, so the voice line about English readers should not be read as a first-ever claim.

Check the exact wording and punctuation of Max Müller's Dhammapada 5 (SBE 10, 1881): 'For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.' The script reads the dash as a semicolon in speech.
Fausbøll's Sutta Nipata is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing from it is quoted; all Sutta Nipata material in this block is paraphrased.
Confirm the count of about seventy suttas (commonly 71 or 72 depending on division) and the chapter names Atthakavagga and Parayanavagga.
The dating claims are presented as a common scholarly view with caution noted.
